## 5. Detailed Findings

### SEC-01: Password change does not revoke existing sessions
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-613: Insufficient Session Expiration
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/CredentialRepository.java:60-74` (caller: `src/main/java/com/example/auth/AdminCli.java:112-116`)

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/example/auth/CredentialRepository.java:60-74
    public void saveCredential(Connection connection, String email, String encodedHash)
            throws SQLException {
        try (PreparedStatement update = connection.prepareStatement(UPSERT)) {
            update.setString(1, encodedHash);
            update.setString(2, email);
            if (update.executeUpdate() > 0) {
                return;
            }
        }
        try (PreparedStatement insert = connection.prepareStatement(INSERT)) {
            insert.setString(1, email);
            insert.setString(2, encodedHash);
            insert.executeUpdate();
        }
    }
```

**Why it is a problem:** Sessions are server-side rows in `user_session` and are only
invalidated by expiry (`expires_at`), explicit `SessionService.revoke`, or the account
becoming inactive. Changing a password writes a new `password_hash` and nothing else, so
every session issued under the old password stays valid for the rest of its TTL (up to
`AUTH_SESSION_TTL_SECONDS`, bounded at 86,400 s). A password reset is the standard response
to a credential compromise, and here it does not evict the attacker: a stolen token
continues to resolve to the user via `SessionService.resolveUserId`. Nothing else in the
code closes this gap — `SessionService.revoke` exists but is never called from the
credential-write path (and is not wired into `App` at all).

**Fix:** Revoke the user's sessions in the same transaction that writes the new hash, so
the change and the eviction are atomic. Capture the affected `user_id` and mark its
sessions revoked (or delete them).

```java
    private static final String REVOKE_ALL_FOR_EMAIL =
            "UPDATE user_session SET revoked_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP "
            + "WHERE revoked_at IS NULL AND user_id = "
            + "(SELECT user_id FROM app_user WHERE email = ?)";

    /**
     * Creates or replaces a user's password hash and revokes every session that was
     * issued under the previous password, in the caller's transaction.
     */
    public void saveCredential(Connection connection, String email, String encodedHash)
            throws SQLException {
        boolean updated;
        try (PreparedStatement update = connection.prepareStatement(UPSERT)) {
            update.setString(1, encodedHash);
            update.setString(2, email);
            updated = update.executeUpdate() > 0;
        }
        if (!updated) {
            try (PreparedStatement insert = connection.prepareStatement(INSERT)) {
                insert.setString(1, email);
                insert.setString(2, encodedHash);
                insert.executeUpdate();
            }
            return; // a new account has no prior sessions
        }
        try (PreparedStatement revoke = connection.prepareStatement(REVOKE_ALL_FOR_EMAIL)) {
            revoke.setString(1, email);
            revoke.executeUpdate();
        }
    }
```

### SEC-02: Database connection never requires TLS; cleartext JDBC URLs are accepted
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-319: Cleartext Transmission of Sensitive Information
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/AuthConfig.java:28-29`, used at `src/main/java/com/example/auth/Database.java:30`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/example/auth/AuthConfig.java:28-29
    private static final Pattern JDBC_URL =
            Pattern.compile("^jdbc:(postgresql|h2):[A-Za-z0-9_:;,.=&/?@\\-]{1,480}$");
```

**Why it is a problem:** The URL allowlist happily matches a remote, unencrypted
connection such as `jdbc:postgresql://db.internal:5432/auth`, and neither `AuthConfig` nor
`Database.openTransaction` (`Database.java:30`) sets or requires `sslmode=verify-full`.
The PostgreSQL JDBC driver's default `sslmode` is `prefer`, which silently falls back to
plaintext and performs no certificate verification even when TLS is negotiated. Everything
this component sends over that link is sensitive: the database password supplied as a
driver property (`Database.java:26-29`), the normalised email addresses used as query
parameters, the stored PBKDF2 hashes returned by `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, and the SHA-256
session-token hashes written by `SessionService.issue` — a token hash observed on the wire
is directly usable to look up or revoke that session, and the password hashes are offline
crackable. The component validates this value carefully for shape but never for the one
property that protects it in transit.

**Fix:** Require transport security for any non-embedded URL: reject a remote PostgreSQL
URL that does not carry `sslmode=verify-full` (and restrict the plaintext exemption to
embedded H2 `mem:`/`file:` URLs), or set the property explicitly in `Database` so the
driver cannot fall back.

```java
    private static final Pattern JDBC_URL =
            Pattern.compile("^jdbc:(postgresql|h2):[A-Za-z0-9_:;,.=&/?@\\-]{1,480}$");

    /** Embedded H2 is local-only; anything else crosses a network and must be encrypted. */
    private static final Pattern LOCAL_EMBEDDED_URL =
            Pattern.compile("^jdbc:h2:(mem|file):[A-Za-z0-9_:;,.=&/?@\\-]{1,470}$");

    private static void requireEncryptedTransport(String url, String lowered) {
        if (LOCAL_EMBEDDED_URL.matcher(url).matches()) {
            return;
        }
        if (!lowered.contains("sslmode=verify-full")) {
            throw new ConfigException(
                    "AUTH_DB_URL must specify sslmode=verify-full for a networked database");
        }
    }
```

### SEC-03: Dangerous JDBC URL options contained by an incomplete denylist
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-184: Incomplete List of Disallowed Inputs
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/AuthConfig.java:36-39`, enforced at `src/main/java/com/example/auth/AuthConfig.java:72-77`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/example/auth/AuthConfig.java:36-39
    private static final String[] FORBIDDEN_URL_TOKENS = {
            "init=", "runscript", "trace_level", "script_", "shutdown",
            "allowothersettings", "socketfactory", "loggerfile", "sslfactory",
    };
```

**Why it is a problem:** The comment above this array states the goal correctly — "a single
mis-set variable should not turn into code execution" — but the control is a denylist of
nine substrings, so it only stops the parameters the author happened to think of. The
allowing regex at line 29 permits arbitrary `;key=value` and `?key=value` sub-options, and
several equally dangerous ones are not listed. On PostgreSQL JDBC,
`sslhostnameverifier=<class>` and `authenticationPluginClassName=<class>` both cause the
driver to load and instantiate a named class from the classpath, and
`sslpassword`/`sslkey`/`sslcert` redirect which key material is used; on H2,
`ACCESS_MODE_DATA` and `IFEXISTS` change file handling. A denylist also fails the moment a
driver is upgraded and gains a new parameter, which is exactly the maintenance trap that
makes CWE-184 a design flaw rather than a typo. Because only trusted configuration reaches
here, impact is limited — but the control is presented as a containment boundary and does
not hold as one.

**Fix:** Invert the control: parse the URL's sub-options and accept only an explicit
allowlist of parameter names, rejecting anything unrecognised. The denylist can stay as a
redundant second check.

```java
    /** The only JDBC sub-options this component accepts; anything else is refused. */
    private static final Set<String> ALLOWED_URL_PARAMETERS = Set.of(
            "sslmode", "sslrootcert", "connecttimeout", "sockettimeout",
            "applicationname", "db_close_delay", "mode");

    private static void requireAllowedUrlOptions(String url) {
        int firstOption = url.indexOf(';') < 0 ? url.indexOf('?') : url.indexOf(';');
        if (firstOption < 0) {
            return; // no sub-options at all
        }
        for (String option : url.substring(firstOption + 1).split("[;&?]")) {
            if (option.isBlank()) {
                continue;
            }
            int eq = option.indexOf('=');
            String name = (eq < 0 ? option : option.substring(0, eq))
                    .trim().toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT);
            if (!ALLOWED_URL_PARAMETERS.contains(name)) {
                throw new ConfigException("AUTH_DB_URL contains an unsupported option");
            }
        }
    }
```

### SEC-04: Per-source counter is process-wide and never cleared, producing a deployment-wide lockout
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-645: Overly Restrictive Account Lockout Mechanism
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/AuthService.java:165-168` (source value from `src/main/java/com/example/auth/AuthConfig.java:88` via `src/main/java/com/example/auth/App.java:45`)

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/example/auth/AuthService.java:165-168
                // Only the account counter is cleared. The source counter deliberately
                // survives a success, so holding one valid account cannot be used to
                // reset a spraying quota.
                throttle.clear(connection, LoginThrottle.Scope.ACCOUNT, email);
```

**Why it is a problem:** The source counter surviving a success is a sound anti-spraying
choice *only* if the source identifier is per-caller. It is not: `AUTH_SOURCE_ID` is a
single environment variable read once at startup (`AuthConfig.java:88`, default
`"local-cli"`) and `App` passes that one constant for every login
(`App.java:45`). All logins served by a deployment therefore share one `SOURCE` bucket of
`AUTH_MAX_ATTEMPTS_PER_SOURCE` attempts (default 30) per window (default 900 s). Once any
30 attempts in the window fail — which any unauthenticated party can cause —
`LoginThrottle.registerAttempt` returns false for every subsequent login from that
deployment, including ones with correct credentials, as the project's own smoke test
demonstrates for the account scope (`scripts/smoke-test.sh:63-72`). The rate limiter thus
becomes a cheap, remotely triggerable denial of service against all users, which is
precisely the outcome `LoginThrottle`'s own class comment says it set out to avoid
("cannot use our own limit as a denial-of-service tool") for the account scope.

**Fix:** Require the source identifier to be the actual per-request caller (the remote
address or client id) rather than a process-wide constant, and refuse to start when a
multi-user deployment is configured with the shared default. Keep the "not cleared on
success" semantics, which are correct once the key is per-caller.

```java
    /**
     * @param rawSource identifier of THIS request's origin (remote network address or
     *                  client id). It must vary per caller: a process-wide constant would
     *                  make the per-source limit a deployment-wide lockout.
     */
    public AuthResult authenticate(String rawEmail, char[] password, String rawSource) {
        if (rawSource != null && rawSource.equals(config.sourceId())
                && !config.singleUserCli()) {
            // Fail closed rather than meter every user through one shared bucket.
            hasher.verifyDecoy(password);
            LOG.severe("Login rejected: AUTH_SOURCE_ID is shared by all callers; "
                    + "pass the per-request source identifier instead");
            return AuthResult.failure(AuthResult.Reason.INVALID_INPUT);
        }
        // ... unchanged ...
    }
```

### SEC-05: Setting a password silently re-activates a deactivated account
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-284: Improper Access Control
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/CredentialRepository.java:19-20`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/example/auth/CredentialRepository.java:19-20
    private static final String UPSERT =
            "UPDATE app_user SET password_hash = ?, is_active = TRUE WHERE email = ?";
```

**Why it is a problem:** `is_active = FALSE` is the component's only account-disable
control: it is what stops authentication (`AuthService.java:151`) and what invalidates
existing sessions (`SessionService.SELECT_ACTIVE` requires `u.is_active = TRUE`). This
statement, reached from `AdminCli set-password`, resets that flag to `TRUE` as an
undocumented side effect of a password change. An operator rotating the password of an
account that was deliberately suspended — a common step while investigating a compromised
account — silently un-suspends it and restores login and session capability. The two
operations (set a credential, change an account's state) should not be coupled, and the
coupling is in the direction that grants access.

**Fix:** Change only the credential; make reactivation a separate, explicit operation.

```java
    private static final String UPSERT =
            "UPDATE app_user SET password_hash = ? WHERE email = ?";
```

### SEC-06: Unsalted SHA-256 used to pseudonymise email addresses in the throttle table and logs
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-328: Use of Weak Hash
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/LoginThrottle.java:63` and `:153`; `src/main/java/com/example/auth/LogMasker.java:23-31`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/example/auth/LoginThrottle.java:63
        String key = Hashing.sha256Hex(scope.name() + ':' + rawKey);
```

**Why it is a problem:** `LoginThrottle`'s class comment claims "the table holds no
addresses or email addresses", and `README.md:139` claims the log fingerprint is "not
enough to recover the address". Neither holds: the input is a low-entropy value from a
small, guessable domain (an email address or an IP address) hashed with a single unsalted,
unkeyed SHA-256. Anyone who reads the `login_throttle` table or the logs — a DBA, a
log-aggregation tenant, or an attacker with read-only database access obtained through
SEC-02 — can confirm whether a specific address has been attempted, or recover addresses
wholesale by hashing a candidate list at billions of guesses per second.
`LogMasker.fingerprint` is worse: it truncates to 48 bits, so it is both reversible by
dictionary and subject to collisions. This is a privacy/claim-accuracy gap, not an
authentication bypass.

**Fix:** Use a keyed hash (HMAC-SHA-256 under a secret pepper from the same configuration
path as the DB password) so the mapping cannot be recomputed without the key, and keep the
full width for the correlation id.

```java
// Hashing.java - add a keyed variant and use it for all pseudonymisation
    static String hmacSha256Hex(byte[] key, String input) {
        try {
            javax.crypto.Mac mac = javax.crypto.Mac.getInstance("HmacSHA256");
            mac.init(new javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec(key, "HmacSHA256"));
            return toHex(mac.doFinal(input.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)));
        } catch (java.security.GeneralSecurityException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("HMAC-SHA-256 is required by the platform", e);
        }
    }

// LoginThrottle.java:63
        String key = Hashing.hmacSha256Hex(pepper, scope.name() + ':' + rawKey);
```

### SEC-07: Database password copied into an immutable `String`, and cleanup bypassed by `System.exit`
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-316: Cleartext Storage of Sensitive Information in Memory
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/Database.java:26-31` (cleanup bypassed at `src/main/java/com/example/auth/App.java:53` and `:55`)

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/example/auth/Database.java:26-31
        char[] password = config.dbPassword();
        if (password.length > 0) {
            props.setProperty("password", new String(password));
        }
        Connection connection = DriverManager.getConnection(config.jdbcUrl(), props);
        props.clear();
```

**Why it is a problem:** The component goes to real lengths to keep secrets in `char[]` so
they can be zeroed (`AuthConfig.close`, `App`'s `finally`, `PBEKeySpec.clearPassword`), and
this line discards that for the database password: `new String(password)` creates an
immutable copy that cannot be wiped and that `props.clear()` does not erase — it only drops
the reference. The copy is created on every `openTransaction()` call, so a long-running
process accumulates unwiped copies on the heap until GC, where a heap dump or core file
discloses them. The same class of gap exists in `App`: `System.exit(0)`/`System.exit(1)` at
`App.java:53` and `App.java:55` are inside the try-with-resources, so neither
`AuthConfig.close()` (which zeroes the DB password) nor the `finally` block at
`App.java:64-68` (which zeroes the user's password array) ever runs on the normal exit
paths.

**Fix:** Build the property value without an extra copy where the driver allows it, and set
exit status through a variable so the resource and `finally` cleanup actually executes.

```java
// Database.java - no retained String copy
        char[] password = config.dbPassword();
        if (password.length > 0) {
            // Properties.put accepts the char[] the JDBC drivers also accept, so no
            // immutable copy of the secret is created.
            props.put("password", password.clone());
        }
        Connection connection = DriverManager.getConnection(config.jdbcUrl(), props);
        Object stored = props.remove("password");
        if (stored instanceof char[] copy) {
            java.util.Arrays.fill(copy, '\0');
        }

// App.java - let try-with-resources and finally run before exiting
        int status = 2;
        try (AuthConfig config = AuthConfig.fromEnvironment(); ConsoleIo io = new ConsoleIo()) {
            // ... unchanged ...
            status = result.isAuthenticated() ? 0 : 1;
        } finally {
            if (password != null) {
                Arrays.fill(password, '\0');
            }
        }
        System.exit(status);
```

### SEC-08: Non-TTY fallback echoes the password and leaves it in an unwipeable `String`
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-549: Missing Password Field Masking
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/ConsoleIo.java:43-52`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/example/auth/ConsoleIo.java:43-52
        System.out.println("Warning: no terminal attached; the password will be echoed.");
        System.out.print(prompt);
        System.out.flush();
        String line = reader.readLine();
        if (line == null) {
            return new char[0];
        }
        char[] value = line.toCharArray();
        // The String copy cannot be wiped; this path is for non-interactive testing only.
        return bound(value);
```

**Why it is a problem:** When `System.console()` returns null the password is read through a
`BufferedReader` into a `String`, so it is echoed (if the input is a terminal that the JVM
simply did not detect, e.g. under some CI and container runtimes) and lands in an immutable
object that the careful `Arrays.fill` cleanup elsewhere cannot reach; the `BufferedReader`'s
internal buffer retains it too. The code documents the limitation and the smoke test needs
this path, but nothing restricts it to testing: the same build will silently take this
branch in production when no console is attached, which is the normal case for a service or
a cron job. A deployment that pipes a password into `App` is a supported-looking mode that
quietly loses the protection.

**Fix:** Require an explicit opt-in for the unmasked path so it cannot be entered by
accident in production, and read it without an intermediate `String`.

```java
    char[] readPassword(String prompt) throws IOException {
        if (console != null) {
            char[] value = console.readPassword("%s", prompt);
            return value == null ? new char[0] : bound(value);
        }
        if (!Boolean.getBoolean("auth.allowUnmaskedPasswordInput")) {
            throw new IOException("no terminal is attached; refusing to read the password "
                    + "unmasked (set -Dauth.allowUnmaskedPasswordInput=true for tests)");
        }
        System.out.println("Warning: no terminal attached; the password will be echoed.");
        System.out.print(prompt);
        System.out.flush();
        char[] buffer = new char[MAX_LINE];
        int n = 0;
        for (int c = reader.read(); c >= 0 && c != '\n' && c != '\r'; c = reader.read()) {
            if (n < buffer.length) {
                buffer[n++] = (char) c;
            }
        }
        char[] value = java.util.Arrays.copyOf(buffer, n);
        java.util.Arrays.fill(buffer, '\0');
        return value;
    }
```

### SEC-09: Silent empty-password fallback for any JDBC URL, including remote databases
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-258: Empty Password in Configuration File
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/AuthConfig.java:151-159`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/example/auth/AuthConfig.java:151-159
        String env = System.getenv("AUTH_DB_PASSWORD");
        if (env != null) {
            if (env.length() > MAX_SECRET_FILE_BYTES) {
                throw new ConfigException("AUTH_DB_PASSWORD is too long");
            }
            return env.toCharArray();
        }
        // Embedded in-memory H2 (demo only) legitimately has no password.
        return new char[0];
```

**Why it is a problem:** The class contract one screen above states "no permissive
fallbacks: a missing or malformed value is a hard startup failure", and this is a
permissive fallback. The empty password is returned for *any* accepted URL, not just the
embedded H2 case the comment describes, so a deployment that sets `AUTH_DB_URL` to a remote
PostgreSQL instance but mis-spells `AUTH_DB_PASSWORD_FILE` (or whose secret-injection
sidecar has not populated it yet) starts up and connects with no password rather than
failing. If that database accepts `trust` or `peer`-style authentication, or the empty
password happens to match, the component runs against it with no credential at all and
nothing in the logs says so. The same branch also returns the password from an environment
variable, which is visible in `/proc/<pid>/environ` and in container inspection output —
acceptable as a documented fallback, but it should not be the silent default.

**Fix:** Allow the empty password only for an embedded H2 URL, and require an explicit
acknowledgement otherwise.

```java
    private static char[] readDbPassword(String jdbcUrl) {
        // ... file and AUTH_DB_PASSWORD branches unchanged ...
        if (LOCAL_EMBEDDED_URL.matcher(jdbcUrl).matches()) {
            return new char[0]; // embedded H2 legitimately has no password
        }
        throw new ConfigException(
                "AUTH_DB_PASSWORD_FILE or AUTH_DB_PASSWORD is required for a networked database");
    }
```

### SEC-10: Permission check and read of the DB password file are not on the same file object
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-367: Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) Race Condition
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/auth/AuthConfig.java:123-131`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/example/auth/AuthConfig.java:123-131
                if (!Files.isRegularFile(path, LinkOption.NOFOLLOW_LINKS)) {
                    throw new ConfigException("AUTH_DB_PASSWORD_FILE is not a regular file");
                }
                if (Files.size(path) > MAX_SECRET_FILE_BYTES) {
                    throw new ConfigException("AUTH_DB_PASSWORD_FILE is larger than "
                            + MAX_SECRET_FILE_BYTES + " bytes");
                }
                requireOwnerOnly(path);
                raw = Files.readAllBytes(path);
```

**Why it is a problem:** Four separate path-based syscalls are performed against the same
name: the type check, the size check and the permission check are `NOFOLLOW_LINKS`, but
`Files.readAllBytes(path)` resolves the name again and *does* follow symlinks. If anything
can modify the containing directory between the check and the read — a co-tenant process,
a secret-injection sidecar, or an operator script with a wider umask — the bytes actually
read may come from a different, symlinked, group-readable, or oversized file than the one
that passed validation. The consequence here is limited (the component would use a wrong
value as the database password and fail to connect, or read a file the validation would
have rejected), but the control as written does not establish the property it claims.

**Fix:** Open the file once and perform every check on that open handle, so the checked
object and the read object are identical.

```java
            try (java.nio.channels.SeekableByteChannel channel = Files.newByteChannel(
                    path, Set.of(StandardOpenOption.READ, LinkOption.NOFOLLOW_LINKS))) {
                PosixFileAttributes attrs = Files.readAttributes(
                        path, PosixFileAttributes.class, LinkOption.NOFOLLOW_LINKS);
                if (!attrs.isRegularFile()) {
                    throw new ConfigException("AUTH_DB_PASSWORD_FILE is not a regular file");
                }
                if (channel.size() > MAX_SECRET_FILE_BYTES) {
                    throw new ConfigException("AUTH_DB_PASSWORD_FILE is larger than "
                            + MAX_SECRET_FILE_BYTES + " bytes");
                }
                requirePermissions(attrs.permissions());
                java.nio.ByteBuffer buffer =
                        java.nio.ByteBuffer.allocate((int) channel.size());
                while (buffer.hasRemaining() && channel.read(buffer) > 0) {
                    // read from the same open handle that was validated
                }
                raw = buffer.array();
            }
```

## 6. Verified Controls and Checks With No Finding

- **SQL injection (first-order), CWE-89:** every statement in the component is a constant
  `String` passed to `prepareStatement` with bound parameters, and no SQL text is built from
  input anywhere — `CredentialRepository.java:16-24` with `setString` at `:41`, `:63-64`,
  `:70-71`; `SessionService.java:31-41` with `setString`/`setLong`/`setObject` at `:60-63`,
  `:82-83`, `:100-101`, `:109`; `LoginThrottle.java:37-49` with binds at `:69-70`, `:85-87`,
  `:116-117`, `:141-144`, `:152-153`, `:168`. Verified by grep that no `Statement.execute`
  takes a concatenated string: the only `createStatement()` use is
  `AdminCli.java:80-83`, which executes the DDL bundled in the artifact's own
  `/schema.sql` resource (`AdminCli.java:73`) and takes no caller-supplied path.
  The smoke test exercises two injection payloads and asserts the table survives
  (`scripts/smoke-test.sh:56-61`).
- **Second-order SQL injection, CWE-89:** values read back out of the database are never
  re-inserted into SQL text. The stored hash is parsed and used only as data
  (`PasswordHasher.java:83-115`), `user_id` is handled as a `long`
  (`CredentialRepository.java:47`, `SessionService.java:88`), and the throttle key is a
  fixed 64-hex digest (`LoginThrottle.java:63`). Returned-column width is additionally
  bounded with `setMaxFieldSize(512)` at `CredentialRepository.java:42`.
- **Password storage, CWE-916/CWE-759/CWE-760:** PBKDF2WithHmacSHA512, 210,000 iterations,
  256-bit output, fresh 16-byte `SecureRandom` salt per hash
  (`PasswordHasher.java:25-34`, `:56-67`). Salts are per-user, not global; iterations are
  recorded in the encoded value with a scheme prefix so re-hashing is possible
  (`PasswordHasher.java:62-63`). No MD5, SHA-1, DES, RC4 or ECB appears anywhere in the
  tree.
- **Hash comparison, CWE-208:** verification uses the platform's constant-time
  `MessageDigest.isEqual` rather than `Arrays.equals` or `String.equals`
  (`PasswordHasher.java:118`).
- **Hostile stored-hash handling, CWE-20:** the encoded value from the database is parsed
  strictly — length ≤ 256, exactly four fields, known scheme id, iterations within
  100,000…5,000,000, salt 8…64 bytes, hash 16…64 bytes — and every failure path performs a
  decoy derivation and returns `false` rather than short-circuiting to success
  (`PasswordHasher.java:77-114`). A KDF that cannot run throws instead of returning a pass
  (`PasswordHasher.java:145-148`).
- **Account enumeration and timing side channels, CWE-203/CWE-204:** a single failure
  message covers every reason (`AuthResult.java:28-30`, `:65-67`), and the no-such-account,
  unusable-hash, invalid-input, unusable-source and throttled paths all spend an equivalent
  PBKDF2 cost via `hasher.verifyDecoy` (`AuthService.java:66`, `:77`, `:88`, `:132`, `:141`);
  a deactivated account is still verified so "disabled" and "wrong password" take the same
  time (`AuthService.java:149-151`). The smoke test asserts the known-account and
  unknown-account outputs are byte-identical (`scripts/smoke-test.sh:52-54`).
- **Session token generation, CWE-330/CWE-338:** 32 bytes (256 bits) from `SecureRandom`,
  base64url-encoded, never derived from or influenced by caller input
  (`SessionService.java:43`, `:54-56`); the raw bytes are zeroed immediately
  (`SessionService.java:57`). No `java.util.Random` is used for any security value — the
  only `ThreadLocalRandom` use is purge sampling (`LoginThrottle.java:164`).
- **Session storage and validation, CWE-384/CWE-613 (partial):** only `SHA-256(token)` is
  persisted (`SessionService.java:60`, `:114-116`), so a database read does not yield usable
  tokens; validation is always a server-side lookup requiring an unrevoked, unexpired row
  joined to an active user (`SessionService.java:34-37`), the token format is checked before
  any database access (`SessionService.java:78-80`, `:96-98`), and a non-positive `user_id`
  is rejected (`SessionService.java:88-89`). TTL is bounded to 60…86,400 s
  (`AuthConfig.java:97`) and expired rows are purged (`SessionService.java:107-112`).
  Revocation on password change is the gap recorded as SEC-01.
- **Cookie attributes, CWE-1004/CWE-614/CWE-1275:** `HttpOnly`, `Secure` and
  `SameSite=Strict` are unconditional with no overload that omits them, the path is
  allowlisted by regex, the token must match the issued format, and `Max-Age` is bounded
  (`SessionCookie.java:19`, `:29-44`); the logout header carries the same attributes
  (`SessionCookie.java:47-52`).
- **Hardcoded credentials, CWE-798/CWE-259:** none in the Java sources, `schema.sql` (which
  seeds no users — `schema.sql:2`), `pom.xml`, or `scripts/smoke-test.sh`, which generates
  its test password at run time into a `umask 077` file and deletes it on exit
  (`scripts/smoke-test.sh:16-29`). The documentation files were grepped for
  password/secret/key/token values and contain only variable names.
- **Credentials on the command line, CWE-214:** `App` refuses all arguments
  (`App.java:31-34`) and `AdminCli set-password` takes only the email and prompts twice for
  the password (`AdminCli.java:98-103`), so no secret reaches the process list.
- **Log redaction, CWE-532:** no password, hash or token is logged; emails are reduced to
  one character plus a fingerprint (`LogMasker.java:15-20`, used at `AuthService.java:79`,
  `:134`, `:143`, `:157`, `:170` and `AdminCli.java:117`), and secrets to a length only
  (`LogMasker.java:34-40`). The smoke test asserts neither the password nor the address
  appears in output (`scripts/smoke-test.sh:74-80`). The hash used for the fingerprint is
  the subject of SEC-06.
- **Error handling / information leakage, CWE-209:** stack traces go to the operator log
  only; the user sees the generic failure text (`AuthService.java:176-179`,
  `App.java:60-63`, `AdminCli.java:52-56`), and configuration errors are reported without
  secret values (`AuthConfig.java:227-231`).
- **Input validation, CWE-20:** email is stripped, bounded to 3…254 chars, restricted to
  printable ASCII, required to have exactly one `@` with RFC-5321 part lengths, matched
  against an anchored pattern, then lower-cased (`InputValidator.java:41-66`); password is
  bounded to 8…256 chars with control characters rejected
  (`InputValidator.java:72-84`); source id is an anchored `[A-Za-z0-9.:_-]{1,64}`
  (`InputValidator.java:86-88`). Input lines are length-capped at read time
  (`ConsoleIo.java:20`, `:55-67`).
- **Unbounded resource consumption, CWE-770:** password length is capped before hashing, the
  throttle key space is bounded by hashing invalid addresses to a single constant
  (`AuthService.java:73`), the throttle and session tables are purged
  (`LoginThrottle.java:162-171`, `SessionService.java:107-112`), and secret files are capped
  at 4,096 bytes (`AuthConfig.java:41`, `:126-129`).
- **Race conditions in the authentication decision, CWE-362:** the credential row is locked
  with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` (`CredentialRepository.java:17`) and the verify-then-issue
  sequence runs inside that same transaction (`AuthService.java:126-169`), so a concurrent
  password change or deactivation cannot interleave. The throttle read-modify-write is also
  row-locked (`LoginThrottle.java:37-39`, `:68-78`) with a savepoint around the insert race
  (`LoginThrottle.java:83-95`), and attempts are committed in their own transaction before
  verification so a later failure cannot reset the counter (`AuthService.java:98-123`).
- **Fail-closed behaviour, CWE-636:** an unattributable source is refused
  (`AuthService.java:63-69`), throttle-accounting errors return a failure rather than
  proceeding (`AuthService.java:119-122`), an unreadable counter row refuses the attempt
  (`LoginThrottle.java:119-121`), and a malformed credential row is treated as unusable
  rather than as a pass (`CredentialRepository.java:50-53`).
- **New-password policy, CWE-521:** minimum 12 characters plus at least three character
  classes on set/change (`AdminCli.java:104-111`, `:153-171`), with the login-time minimum
  deliberately kept lower so legacy passwords are not locked out
  (`InputValidator.java:17-22`). No breached-password or common-password check is performed;
  that is a hardening recommendation, not a finding.
- **Session token file permissions, CWE-276/CWE-59:** the file is created with `0600` in a
  single `CREATE_NEW` open, a non-regular path (symlink) is refused, and the terminal shows
  only a masked form (`App.java:93-114`, `:71-84`); `CREATE_NEW` maps to `O_CREAT|O_EXCL`,
  so a pre-planted symlink causes a failure rather than a redirected write. The smoke test
  asserts mode 600 (`scripts/smoke-test.sh:44-45`).
- **DB password file permissions, CWE-732:** group/other read and write are rejected
  outright (`AuthConfig.java:162-178`); the residual issue is only the check/use race in
  SEC-10.
- **Path traversal, CWE-22:** the two caller-influenced paths are absolutised and
  normalised and are used only as whole file names, never joined with other input
  (`AuthConfig.java:106`, `:120`); the schema is loaded from the artifact's own classpath
  resource, not a caller-supplied path (`AdminCli.java:73`).
- **Insecure deserialization, CWE-502:** no Java serialization, XML, YAML or object-graph
  deserialization anywhere; the only parsed external formats are Base64 inside the
  strictly-bounded hash parser and `Integer.parseInt` on bounded configuration values.
- **OS command execution, CWE-78:** no `Runtime.exec`, `ProcessBuilder`, or shell invocation
  in the Java sources. `scripts/smoke-test.sh` runs under `set -euo pipefail` with every
  expansion quoted and a `trap`-cleaned `mktemp -d` work directory
  (`scripts/smoke-test.sh:5-18`).
- **XSS / template injection / SSRF / XXE / open redirect:** not applicable — the component
  renders no markup, evaluates no templates, makes no outbound HTTP request, parses no XML,
  and performs no redirects. Confirmed by grep for `URL`, `HttpClient`, `openStream`,
  `DocumentBuilder` and template APIs across `src/`.
- **Dependency / supply-chain posture, CWE-1104:** a single runtime-scoped dependency pinned
  to an exact version (H2 2.3.232, `pom.xml:17`, `:25-30`) with all cryptography taken from
  the JDK; compiler release pinned to 17 with `-Xlint:all` (`pom.xml:38-46`). No automated
  CVE gate (OWASP dependency-check / `mvn versions`) is wired into the build — a hardening
  recommendation, not a finding.
- **Schema constraints, CWE-20:** unique email, `NOT NULL` hash, bounded column widths
  matching the application's own limits, FK with `ON DELETE CASCADE`, and a composite
  primary key on the throttle scope (`schema.sql:4-30`).


---

### 10) results-cyber/claude/claude/set_a/post_research/4/security/security_review.md

# Security Review: secure-accounts (local account registration, login and session CLI)

## 1. Executive Summary

`secure-accounts` is a small Java 17 Maven project that implements local account
registration, password authentication and server-side session management on top of a
SQLite database, driven by a four-command CLI (`register`, `login`, `whoami`, `logout`).

The code is defensively written and the high-risk classics are genuinely absent: every
SQL statement is a `PreparedStatement` with bound parameters (no string-built SQL
anywhere), passwords are stored as Argon2id PHC strings with a 16-byte `SecureRandom`
salt, hash comparison is `MessageDigest.isEqual`, session tokens are 256-bit CSPRNG
values stored only as SHA-256 digests and validated exclusively against server-side
state, there are no hardcoded secrets, and user-facing messages are deliberately
uniform so registration and login leak no account-existence oracle.

No critical or high-severity vulnerability was found. The findings below are one
medium-severity file-permission weakness and a set of low-severity hardening gaps:

- **SEC-01 (Medium)** the SQLite database holding password hashes is created under the
  process umask and only chmod-ed to `0600` *after* the schema migration has run.
- **SEC-02 … SEC-08 (Low)** terminal detection that no longer holds on modern JREs,
  an unsalted digest of login identifiers, a fixed- rather than sliding-window rate
  limiter, a client-overridable rate-limit source key, acceptance of out-of-policy
  Argon2 cost parameters from stored hashes, no session rotation/revocation on a new
  login, and a 20-entry stub password blocklist.

## 2. Scope

| File | Purpose | Security-relevant behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/App.java` | CLI front end for the four commands | Reads passwords from the terminal/stdin, writes and reads the session token file (`0600`), masks user-facing errors, derives the rate-limit source id, wipes secrets in `finally` |
| `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/AccountService.java` | Registration and authentication orchestration | Enumeration-resistant ordering, decoy-hash work equalisation, throttle gating, session issue, identifier canonicalisation, log masking |
| `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/PasswordHasher.java` | Argon2id hashing in PHC format | KDF parameters, `SecureRandom` salt, constant-time compare, strict parsing of stored hashes, pepper as Argon2 secret, buffer wiping |
| `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/SessionService.java` | Server-side session storage | 32-byte CSPRNG token, SHA-256-at-rest, idle/absolute expiry, revocation, strict token format check, pruning |
| `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/SessionCookie.java` | `Set-Cookie` builder for an HTTP front end | `__Host-` prefix, `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict`, `Path=/`, no `Domain` |
| `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/ThrottleService.java` | Login/registration attempt counting | Per-source and per-account counters, digest-keyed rows, atomic check-and-increment, window expiry, pruning |
| `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/AccountRepository.java` | All SQL on the `account` table | Parameterised insert/select/update, uniqueness via DB constraint, `SQLState` 23 duplicate detection |
| `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/Database.java` | Connection factory, migration, transactions | `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transactions, rollback on failure, schema with `CHECK`/`UNIQUE` constraints, database file permissions |
| `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/InputValidator.java` | Validation/canonicalisation of email, username, password | Allowlist character checks, length bounds, NFKC/NFC normalisation, reserved names, password policy and blocklist |
| `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/Config.java` | Environment-driven configuration | Range-checked settings, allowlisted JDBC prefix, pepper from env only, owner-only data directory, secret-free `toString` |
| `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/Logging.java` | Single application logger | `0600` log file, symlink refusal, one-line formatter that neutralises injected newlines |
| `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/Mask.java` | Masking for log/console output | Email/username masking, JDBC URL credential stripping |
| `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/Wipe.java` | Zeroing of `char[]`/`byte[]` credential buffers | Best-effort secret erasure |
| `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/Hex.java` | Lowercase hex encoding | Encoding of digests and session references |
| `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/ValidationException.java` | Format-only error type | Messages must not reflect server-side state |
| `pom.xml` | Build and dependency pinning | Pinned Bouncy Castle 1.79 / sqlite-jdbc 3.47.1.0, HTTPS-only Maven Central with `checksumPolicy=fail`, no snapshots |

Test sources under `src/test` and build output under `target/` were read for context but
are not production attack surface and produced no findings.

## 3. Skills Applied

- `review-code-for-security-vulnerabilities`: router skill — drove the file-by-file
  behaviour inventory and the selection of the specialised skills below.
- `performing-cryptographic-audit-of-application`: applied to `PasswordHasher`,
  `SessionService`, `ThrottleService` and `Config` — deprecated algorithms (none: no
  MD5/SHA-1/DES/RC4/ECB), KDF parameter strength, salt/IV handling, RNG choice,
  hardcoded-secret scan (none found), key/pepper storage and wiping. Fired on SEC-03
  and SEC-06.
- `testing-api-authentication-weaknesses`: applied to `AccountService`,
  `SessionService` and `SessionCookie` — token entropy, expiration, server-side
  revocation, logout behaviour, session rotation, password policy and credential-stuffing
  resistance. Fired on SEC-07 and SEC-08.
- `testing-for-sensitive-data-exposure`: applied to `Database`, `Logging`, `Mask`,
  `Config` and the session-token file handling in `App` — data at rest, secret leakage
  into logs/messages/arguments, masking and redaction, file permissions. Fired on
  SEC-01 and SEC-02.
- `implementing-api-rate-limiting-and-throttling` and `performing-api-rate-limiting-bypass`:
  applied to `ThrottleService` and `AccountService.normalizeSourceId` — window algorithm
  choice, counter atomicity, per-source vs per-account scoping, source-identifier
  trustworthiness, lockout-as-DoS. Fired on SEC-04 and SEC-05.
- `exploiting-sql-injection-vulnerabilities` / `performing-second-order-sql-injection`:
  applied to `AccountRepository`, `SessionService` and `ThrottleService` — no finding
  (see section 6).
- `exploiting-race-condition-vulnerabilities`: applied to `Database.inTransaction`,
  `ThrottleService.tryAcquire` and `AccountRepository.insert` — TOCTOU on
  check-then-act sequences; no finding (see section 6).
- Reviewed against general OWASP Top 10 / CWE knowledge, because no library skill
  matched these behaviours directly: Unicode canonicalisation and homograph collisions
  in `InputValidator` (NFKC-before-casefold, ASCII allowlist), log-injection via
  `Logging.PlainFormatter.oneLine` (CWE-117), symlink/TOCTOU handling on the data
  directory, log file and session-token file (CWE-59/CWE-367), terminal secret input
  handling, generic-error / account-enumeration behaviour (CWE-204), dependency and
  build provenance in `pom.xml` (no known-vulnerable pinned versions identified), and
  insecure deserialization (none: no Java serialization, XML or object parsing exists
  in the codebase).

## 5. Detailed Findings

### SEC-01: Database file containing password hashes is created with umask permissions and only restricted after migration
- **Severity:** Medium
- **CWE:** CWE-732: Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/Database.java:53-54`, `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/Database.java:103-124`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/example/accounts/Database.java:52-56
        Database db = new Database(url, props, log);
        db.migrate();
        db.restrictDatabaseFilePermissions(url);
        log.info(() -> "database ready at " + Mask.jdbcUrl(url));
        return db;
```
```java
// src/main/java/com/example/accounts/Database.java:117-123
            Path p = suffix.isEmpty() ? base : Paths.get(pathPart + suffix);
            try {
                if (Files.exists(p) && !Files.isSymbolicLink(p)
                        && p.getFileSystem().supportedFileAttributeViews().contains("posix")) {
                    Files.setPosixFilePermissions(p, PosixFilePermissions.fromString("rw-------"));
                }
            } catch (IOException | UnsupportedOperationException e) {
```

**Why it is a problem:** `migrate()` is what causes SQLite to create `accounts.db` (and its
`-wal`/`-shm` siblings, which inherit the main file's mode), so the file that holds every
Argon2 hash and session digest is created with the process umask — typically `0644`,
world-readable — and is only tightened afterwards. Every other sensitive file in this
project is created tightly *first* (`Logging.openPrivateFileHandler` at
`src/main/java/com/example/accounts/Logging.java:64-69` and `App.storeSessionToken` at
`src/main/java/com/example/accounts/App.java:330-335` both pass
`PosixFilePermissions.asFileAttribute`), so this path is the inconsistent one. The default
database lives inside the `0700` data directory, which contains the exposure, but
`ACCOUNTS_JDBC_URL` is only prefix-checked (`src/main/java/com/example/accounts/Config.java:160`)
and may legitimately point anywhere, e.g. `jdbc:sqlite:/var/tmp/accounts.db`, where the
window is directly exploitable by any local user who opens or hard-links the file during
migration. Relatedly, the `isSymbolicLink` guard here runs *after* SQLite has already
opened and followed the path, so it protects the `chmod` but not the write.

**Fix:** Create the database file with owner-only permissions before any connection opens
it, and keep the post-migration tightening as a belt-and-braces step.
```java
    public static Database open(Config config, Logger log) throws SQLException {
        String url = config.jdbcUrl();
        if (!url.startsWith("jdbc:sqlite:")) {
            throw new SQLException("unsupported JDBC URL");
        }
        Properties props = new Properties();
        props.setProperty("foreign_keys", "true");
        props.setProperty("journal_mode", "WAL");
        props.setProperty("synchronous", "NORMAL");
        props.setProperty("busy_timeout", "5000");
        props.setProperty("transaction_mode", "IMMEDIATE");
        Database db = new Database(url, props, log);
        db.precreateDatabaseFileOwnerOnly(url);   // 0600 before SQLite ever opens it
        db.migrate();
        db.restrictDatabaseFilePermissions(url);  // still re-asserted afterwards
        log.info(() -> "database ready at " + Mask.jdbcUrl(url));
        return db;
    }

    /** Creates an empty 0600 database file if absent, so SQLite never widens it. */
    private void precreateDatabaseFileOwnerOnly(String url) {
        String pathPart = databasePath(url); // extracted from restrictDatabaseFilePermissions
        if (pathPart == null) {
            return; // in-memory database, nothing on disk
        }
        Path p = Paths.get(pathPart);
        try {
            if (Files.isSymbolicLink(p)) {
                throw new IOException("database path is a symbolic link");
            }
            if (!Files.exists(p)
                    && p.getFileSystem().supportedFileAttributeViews().contains("posix")) {
                Files.createFile(p, PosixFilePermissions.asFileAttribute(
                        PosixFilePermissions.fromString("rw-------")));
            }
        } catch (IOException | UnsupportedOperationException e) {
            log.log(Level.WARNING, "could not pre-create database file with 0600", e);
        }
    }
```

### SEC-02: Secret input gate relies on `System.console() != null` as a terminal test
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-549: Missing Password Field Masking
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/App.java:306-317`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/example/accounts/App.java:306-317
    private static char[] readSecret(String label) throws IOException {
        if (System.console() != null) {
            return System.console().readPassword("%s", label);
        }
        if (!"true".equalsIgnoreCase(System.getenv("ACCOUNTS_PASSWORD_STDIN"))) {
            throw new IOException("no terminal available for password entry; "
                    + "set ACCOUNTS_PASSWORD_STDIN=true to read it from standard input");
        }
        // Read into a char[] rather than a String, which could not be wiped afterwards. One extra
        // character of headroom so an over-long password is seen and rejected, not truncated.
        return readLine(stdin(), InputValidator.PASSWORD_MAX_LENGTH + 1);
    }
```

**Why it is a problem:** The whole design rests on "console present implies a real terminal
with echo control". That was true on the JDK 17 this project targets, but from JDK 22
onwards `System.console()` returns a `Console` even when the standard streams are
redirected or attached to a non-echo-controllable virtual terminal, which is exactly why
`Console.isTerminal()` was added. The jar is a shaded executable that will be run on
whatever JRE is installed. On a newer JRE the first branch is taken unconditionally: the
explicit `ACCOUNTS_PASSWORD_STDIN` opt-in that the class documentation presents as the only
way a secret may come from stdin is silently bypassed, echo suppression is not guaranteed
(so the password can appear on screen and in terminal scrollback), and the returned array is
not length-bounded by `readLine`.

**Fix:** Test for an actual terminal, not merely for the presence of a `Console`, and keep
the stdin path behind its opt-in.
```java
    private static char[] readSecret(String label) throws IOException {
        if (isInteractiveTerminal()) {
            return System.console().readPassword("%s", label);
        }
        if (!"true".equalsIgnoreCase(System.getenv("ACCOUNTS_PASSWORD_STDIN"))) {
            throw new IOException("no terminal available for password entry; "
                    + "set ACCOUNTS_PASSWORD_STDIN=true to read it from standard input");
        }
        return readLine(stdin(), InputValidator.PASSWORD_MAX_LENGTH + 1);
    }

    /**
     * True only for a real echo-controllable terminal. On JDK 22+ System.console() is
     * non-null even for redirected streams, so isTerminal() is the load-bearing check;
     * it is called reflectively so the code still compiles and runs on JDK 17.
     */
    private static boolean isInteractiveTerminal() {
        java.io.Console console = System.console();
        if (console == null) {
            return false;
        }
        try {
            return (boolean) java.io.Console.class.getMethod("isTerminal").invoke(console);
        } catch (ReflectiveOperationException | RuntimeException e) {
            return true; // pre-JDK 22: a non-null Console already implies a terminal
        }
    }
```

### SEC-03: Login identifiers are keyed with an unsalted SHA-256 whose pepper is optional
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-916: Use of Password Hash With Insufficient Computational Effort
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/ThrottleService.java:190-204`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/example/accounts/ThrottleService.java:190-204
    private String key(String scope, String identifier) {
        MessageDigest digest;
        try {
            digest = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256");
        } catch (NoSuchAlgorithmException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("SHA-256 unavailable", e);
        }
        if (pepper.length > 0) {
            digest.update(pepper);
        }
        digest.update(scope.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
        digest.update((byte) ':');
        digest.update(identifier.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
        return Hex.encode(digest.digest());
    }
```

**Why it is a problem:** The class documentation claims the `auth_attempt` table "is not a
log of who tried to log in from where" (`src/main/java/com/example/accounts/ThrottleService.java:28-30`),
but the pepper is optional and empty by default (`src/main/java/com/example/accounts/Config.java:165-168`).
With no pepper the key is a plain, unsalted SHA-256 over a low-entropy value — an email
address or an IP string — so anyone who reads the database can recover the exact identifiers
by hashing a candidate list (the entire IPv4 space is ~4 billion digests, and breached email
lists are free). The protection the comment promises therefore does not exist in the default
configuration, and the inputs are precisely the PII the design set out not to store.

**Fix:** Make the keying secret mandatory for this table rather than optional, and use a
proper keyed MAC instead of a hash-prefix construction.
```java
    private final javax.crypto.SecretKey keyingKey;

    public ThrottleService(Config config) {
        this.config = config;
        byte[] pepper = config.pepper();
        // Fail closed: without a keying secret the stored digests are trivially reversible,
        // so refuse to run rather than silently storing recoverable identifiers.
        if (pepper.length < 16) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(Config.ENV_PEPPER
                    + " is required: it keys the throttle identifier digests");
        }
        this.keyingKey = new javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec(pepper, "HmacSHA256");
    }

    /** Domain-separated HMAC of the identifier; 64 lowercase hex characters. */
    private String key(String scope, String identifier) {
        try {
            javax.crypto.Mac mac = javax.crypto.Mac.getInstance("HmacSHA256");
            mac.init(keyingKey);
            mac.update(scope.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
            mac.update((byte) ':');
            mac.update(identifier.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
            return Hex.encode(mac.doFinal());
        } catch (java.security.GeneralSecurityException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("HmacSHA256 unavailable", e);
        }
    }
```

### SEC-04: Attempt counter is a fixed window, allowing ~2x the configured failures across a boundary
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/ThrottleService.java:57-65`, `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/ThrottleService.java:146-149`

**Vulnerable code:**
```sql
-- src/main/java/com/example/accounts/ThrottleService.java:58-64
            INSERT INTO auth_attempt (scope, scope_key, window_start, failures)
            VALUES (?, ?, ?, 1)
            ON CONFLICT (scope, scope_key) DO UPDATE SET
              window_start = CASE WHEN auth_attempt.window_start <= ? THEN excluded.window_start
                                  ELSE auth_attempt.window_start END,
              failures     = CASE WHEN auth_attempt.window_start <= ? THEN 1
                                  ELSE auth_attempt.failures + 1 END
```

**Why it is a problem:** `window_start` is anchored at the first attempt and the counter is
reset wholesale once that anchor ages past the cutoff, which is a *fixed* window — not the
"short sliding window" the class documentation describes
(`src/main/java/com/example/accounts/ThrottleService.java:21-22`). An attacker who times
their bursts around the boundary gets twice the budget in a short period: with the defaults,
10 guesses against one account at T+14:59 and 10 more at T+15:01 is 20 guesses in two
minutes against a nominal limit of 10 per 15 minutes, and 50 rather than 25 per source. The
same pattern repeats every window, so the sustained bypass factor is the burst factor.

**Fix:** Use a true sliding window — keep the window anchored to the most recent attempt, or
store per-attempt timestamps and count those inside the window.
```sql
            INSERT INTO auth_attempt (scope, scope_key, window_start, failures)
            VALUES (?, ?, ?, 1)
            ON CONFLICT (scope, scope_key) DO UPDATE SET
              -- Slide the window forward on every counted attempt so a burst straddling
              -- the old boundary cannot double the budget.
              window_start = excluded.window_start,
              failures     = CASE WHEN auth_attempt.window_start <= ? THEN 1
                                  ELSE auth_attempt.failures + 1 END
```

### SEC-05: CLI rate-limit source identifier is taken from the overridable `user.name` property
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-807: Reliance on Untrusted Inputs in a Security Decision
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/App.java:239-242`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/example/accounts/App.java:239-242
    private static String sourceId() {
        String user = System.getProperty("user.name");
        return "cli:" + (user == null || user.isBlank() ? "unknown" : user);
    }
```

**Why it is a problem:** `user.name` is an ordinary writable system property, so the person
invoking the jar chooses the value: `java -Duser.name=a1 -jar accounts.jar login`,
`-Duser.name=a2`, and so on each land in a fresh per-source bucket. The per-source counter
is described as "what actually stops credential stuffing"
(`src/main/java/com/example/accounts/ThrottleService.java:17-19`), and here it can be reset
at will by the caller, leaving only the per-account counter. The practical impact is limited
because the default database sits in the invoking user's own `0700` directory, but it becomes
real as soon as the store is shared between local accounts, and it is the same mistake as
trusting `X-Forwarded-For` that `normalizeSourceId` explicitly warns against.

**Fix:** Derive the source from something the caller cannot set, such as the real OS user
behind the process.
```java
    private static String sourceId() {
        // Not user.name: that is a writable system property the caller can rotate with
        // -Duser.name=... to get a fresh rate-limit bucket per attempt.
        String user = System.getenv("USER");
        if (user == null || user.isBlank()) {
            try {
                user = java.nio.file.Files.getOwner(
                        java.nio.file.Paths.get(System.getProperty("java.io.tmpdir"))
                                .getFileSystem().getPath("/proc/self")).getName();
            } catch (IOException | RuntimeException e) {
                user = null;
            }
        }
        return "cli:" + (user == null || user.isBlank() ? "unknown" : user);
    }
```

### SEC-06: Stored-hash parser accepts Argon2 cost parameters far below the configured policy floor
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-916: Use of Password Hash With Insufficient Computational Effort
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/PasswordHasher.java:41-44`, `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/PasswordHasher.java:234-236`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/example/accounts/PasswordHasher.java:40-45
    /** Bounds applied when parsing a stored hash, independent of the configured cost. */
    private static final int MIN_MEMORY_KIB = 8;
    private static final int MAX_MEMORY_KIB = 1_048_576;   // 1 GiB ceiling
    private static final int MAX_ITERATIONS = 20;
    private static final int MAX_PARALLELISM = 16;
    private static final int MAX_ENCODED_LENGTH = 512;
```

**Why it is a problem:** `Config.Argon2Settings` enforces the OWASP floor of
`m>=19456, t>=2` for hashes this code *writes*
(`src/main/java/com/example/accounts/Config.java:77-79`), but `verify` happily honours a
stored `m=8,t=1,p=1` — a KDF roughly four orders of magnitude cheaper than policy. A row
reached through a restored backup, a replication bug or any write primitive short of full
control therefore turns that account's hash into something crackable at near-plaintext
speed, and the cheap verification is also a timing oracle distinguishing such accounts from
normal ones. The upper bounds (the memory-DoS case the comment is aimed at) are handled; the
lower bound is not. `needsRehash` does upgrade the row after a *successful* login, which
limits but does not remove the exposure.

**Fix:** Clamp the accepted parameters to the configured policy floor, so an under-cost row
fails closed like any other unparsable value.
```java
    /** Bounds applied when parsing a stored hash. Floors match the OWASP minimums in Config. */
    private static final int MIN_MEMORY_KIB = 19_456;      // never below the policy floor
    private static final int MIN_ITERATIONS = 2;
    private static final int MAX_MEMORY_KIB = 1_048_576;   // 1 GiB ceiling
    private static final int MAX_ITERATIONS = 20;
    private static final int MAX_PARALLELISM = 16;
    private static final int MAX_ENCODED_LENGTH = 512;

    // ... in parse():
        int memoryKib = parseParam(params[0], "m=", MIN_MEMORY_KIB, MAX_MEMORY_KIB);
        int iterations = parseParam(params[1], "t=", MIN_ITERATIONS, MAX_ITERATIONS);
        int parallelism = parseParam(params[2], "p=", 1, MAX_PARALLELISM);
```

### SEC-07: A new successful login neither rotates nor revokes the previous session
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-613: Insufficient Session Expiration
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/AccountService.java:202-208`, `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/App.java:162`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/example/accounts/AccountService.java:202-208
            SessionService.IssuedSession issued = database.inTransaction(connection -> {
                throttle.clearAccount(connection, lookupKey, now);
                if (upgraded != null) {
                    accounts.updatePasswordHash(connection, accountId, upgraded, now);
                }
                return sessions.issue(connection, accountId, now);
            });
```
```java
// src/main/java/com/example/accounts/App.java:162
                    storeSessionToken(config, session.token());
```

**Why it is a problem:** Each login mints an additional session and the CLI overwrites the
single-slot token file, so the previous token stays valid server-side until its idle or
absolute timeout — up to 12 hours by default — with no way for the user to reach it:
`logout` can only revoke the token currently in the file. `SessionService.revokeAllForAccount`
exists for exactly this purpose and is never called from anywhere in the codebase. A user who
suspects a stolen token and responds by logging in again (the intuitive action) does not
invalidate it, and `updatePasswordHash` likewise rotates the stored hash without revoking
anything.

**Fix:** Revoke the account's existing sessions as part of the same transaction that issues
the new one, before `issue` runs.
```java
            SessionService.IssuedSession issued = database.inTransaction(connection -> {
                throttle.clearAccount(connection, lookupKey, now);
                if (upgraded != null) {
                    accounts.updatePasswordHash(connection, accountId, upgraded, now);
                }
                // A fresh authentication supersedes older sessions: a stolen token must not
                // outlive the login that replaced it (same transaction, so no window).
                sessions.revokeAllForAccount(connection, accountId);
                return sessions.issue(connection, accountId, now);
            });
```

### SEC-08: Breached-password blocklist is a 20-entry stub
- **Severity:** Low
- **CWE:** CWE-521: Weak Password Requirements
- **Location:** `src/main/java/com/example/accounts/InputValidator.java:39-44`

**Vulnerable code:**
```java
// src/main/java/com/example/accounts/InputValidator.java:39-44
    /** A small, high-frequency blocklist; see README for wiring a full breached-password list. */
    private static final Set<String> BLOCKED_PASSWORDS = Set.of(
            "123456789012", "passwordpassword", "password1234", "qwertyuiop12", "administrator",
            "iloveyou1234", "letmein12345", "welcome12345", "monkey123456", "dragon123456",
            "football1234", "baseball1234", "sunshine1234", "princess1234", "qwerty123456",
            "abc123456789", "trustno12345", "changeme1234", "secret123456", "superman1234");
```

**Why it is a problem:** The rest of the policy (12-character minimum, 5 distinct
characters, no username/email substring, no single repeated character, no monotonic run) is
sound, but the breached-credential check — the control that actually matters against
credential stuffing — covers twenty strings matched by exact equality. `Summer2024!`,
`Password123!` and the millions of other known-breached passwords above 12 characters all
pass. The limitation is acknowledged in the README and in the comment, but as shipped the
check provides essentially no coverage, and the per-account rate limit is a 15-minute window
rather than a lockout, so a weak password remains guessable over time.

**Fix:** Check the prepared password against a real breached-password corpus loaded from a
file (or the Pwned Passwords k-anonymity range API), keeping the in-code set only as a
fallback.
```java
    /**
     * Breached-password check against a SHA-1-prefixed corpus (HIBP "Pwned Passwords"
     * format: one UPPERCASE hex digest per line). Path comes from configuration; the
     * small in-code set remains as a fallback when no corpus is installed.
     */
    private static boolean isBreached(char[] prepared, java.nio.file.Path corpus)
            throws java.io.IOException {
        byte[] utf8 = null;
        try {
            utf8 = toUtf8(prepared); // char[] -> byte[], no String materialised
            String digest = Hex.encode(
                    java.security.MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-1").digest(utf8))
                    .toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT);
            try (java.util.stream.Stream<String> lines = java.nio.file.Files.lines(corpus)) {
                return lines.anyMatch(line -> line.startsWith(digest));
            }
        } catch (java.security.NoSuchAlgorithmException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("SHA-1 unavailable", e);
        } finally {
            Wipe.bytes(utf8);
        }
    }
```

## 6. Verified Controls and Checks With No Finding

- **SQL injection (CWE-89):** every statement in the codebase is a constant string with
  bound parameters — `AccountRepository.java:24-38` (`INSERT`/`SELECT`/`UPDATE`),
  `SessionService.java:33-58` (six statements), `ThrottleService.java:53-73` (four
  statements), and the DDL in `Database.java:143-182` contains no interpolation. No
  `Statement.execute(String)` is ever called with a runtime-built string; `createStatement`
  is used only for the constant schema array. Second-order injection was checked too: values
  read back out of the database (`password_hash`, `session_ref`) are never re-concatenated
  into SQL.
- **Password storage (CWE-916/CWE-759):** Argon2id via Bouncy Castle with
  `m=65536, t=3, p=1` defaults validated against the OWASP floor
  (`Config.java:74-80, 92-95`), a fresh 16-byte `SecureRandom` salt per hash
  (`PasswordHasher.java:69-70`), 32-byte output, standard PHC encoding
  (`PasswordHasher.java:191-197`), and an optional pepper supplied as Argon2's *secret*
  parameter rather than concatenated (`PasswordHasher.java:158-160`).
- **Constant-time comparison (CWE-208):** hash equality uses `MessageDigest.isEqual`
  (`PasswordHasher.java:102`); no `Arrays.equals`/`String.equals` on secret material in the
  authentication path.
- **Hash upgrade path:** `needsRehash` compares stored cost against current policy and the
  row is rewritten inside the post-authentication transaction
  (`PasswordHasher.java:111-126`, `AccountService.java:198-206`).
- **Stored-hash parsing as untrusted input (CWE-20):** length cap, exact field count,
  algorithm and version pinning, bounded integer parsing and bounded base64 decoding, with
  every failure returning `false` rather than throwing
  (`PasswordHasher.java:215-280`, `PasswordHasher.java:87-96`).
- **Session token entropy and handling (CWE-330/CWE-384):** 32 bytes from `SecureRandom`
  generated server-side only, never caller-supplied, so no session fixation is possible
  (`SessionService.java:77-84`); only `SHA-256(token)` is persisted
  (`SessionService.java:203-216`); strict fixed-length base64url format check before the
  value reaches any query (`SessionService.java:189-201`).
- **Session expiration and revocation (CWE-613):** idle and absolute expiry plus the
  `revoked` flag are re-checked against the database on every `validate`, and the idle
  refresh happens in the same transaction as the decision
  (`SessionService.java:113-153`); `revoke` is silent for unknown tokens
  (`SessionService.java:159-168`); expired and revoked rows are pruned
  (`SessionService.java:56-58`). See SEC-07 for the one gap.
- **Cookie attributes (CWE-1004/CWE-614/CWE-352):** `__Host-` prefix with `Path=/`, no
  `Domain`, `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict`, and a token-format precondition before
  the header is built (`SessionCookie.java:20, 38-43`).
- **Account enumeration (CWE-204):** registration returns `ACCEPTED` with identical wording
  for created and duplicate (`AccountService.java:126-137`, `App.java:127-132`);
  authentication returns one `INVALID_CREDENTIALS` for unknown identifier, wrong password
  and disabled account (`AccountService.java:174-195`, `App.java:172-176`); unknown
  identifiers still pay for a full Argon2 verification against a decoy hash with current
  parameters (`AccountService.java:86`, `PasswordHasher.java:132-145`), and an unusable
  password input burns comparable work (`AccountService.java:182`, `241-249`). The
  reserved-username message reveals only membership of a static list.
- **Rate limiting scope design (lockout-as-DoS, CWE-645):** both per-source and per-account
  counters exist, the per-account one expires unattended and is cleared by the victim's own
  successful login, blocked attempts are not counted so a window cannot be renewed
  indefinitely, the source counter is deliberately not cleared on success, and registration
  counts against the source only so nobody can burn a victim's account budget
  (`ThrottleService.java:100-135`, `AccountService.java:114-121`).
- **Concurrency / TOCTOU (CWE-367/CWE-362):** `inTransaction` takes the SQLite write lock up
  front via `transaction_mode=IMMEDIATE` with auto-commit off and rolls back on any failure
  (`Database.java:50-56`, `Database.java:77-92`); the throttle check and increment run inside
  the caller's transaction (`ThrottleService.java:100-119`); account uniqueness is decided by
  `UNIQUE` constraints surfaced as a duplicate rather than by read-then-write
  (`AccountRepository.java:50-68`, `Database.java:147-150`).
- **Input validation (CWE-20/CWE-176):** ASCII-only allowlists with length bounds for email
  local part, domain labels and TLD (`InputValidator.java:56-136`); username bounded
  *before* NFKC normalisation then re-bounded after, with a separator-adjacency rule and a
  reserved-name list, which is what stops full-width and compatibility homographs collapsing
  onto an existing name (`InputValidator.java:144-178`); RFC 8265 OpaqueString preparation
  for passwords, rejecting control, format, surrogate, private-use and unassigned code points
  (`InputValidator.java:184-228`).
- **Secrets in source / arguments (CWE-798/CWE-214):** no credential is compiled in (grep for
  hardcoded key/password/token patterns over `src/main/java` returns only comments and
  `SecureRandom` constructions); the pepper comes from the environment only and is never
  logged or echoed on a decode failure (`Config.java:43-44, 165-181`); passwords are never
  accepted as command-line arguments (`App.java:22-26`); `Config.toString` omits the pepper
  (`Config.java:262-271`).
- **Sensitive data in logs (CWE-532/CWE-117):** passwords and raw tokens have no masking
  helper and are never logged (`Mask.java:4-8`); emails and usernames are masked at every log
  site (`AccountService.java:130-135, 192-193, 209-212`); JDBC URLs are stripped of userinfo
  and query strings before logging (`Mask.java:39-59`, `Database.java:55`); the formatter
  collapses CR/LF/NEL/LS/PS so injected newlines cannot forge entries
  (`Logging.java:107-109`); the session token is never printed — only the non-secret reference
  is (`App.java:163-165`).
- **File permissions for log and session files (CWE-732/CWE-59):** both are created with
  `rw-------` as a creation attribute before any write, both refuse a symlinked path, and
  `FileHandler` is deliberately limited to a single file so no rotated world-readable copy is
  produced (`Logging.java:64-80`, `App.java:324-345`); the data directory itself is forced to
  `rwx------` and rejected if it is a symlink (`Config.java:120-151`); the session file is
  size-bounded before being read (`App.java:347-356`).
- **Secret lifetime in memory (CWE-316):** passwords and tokens are handled as `char[]`/
  `byte[]` and zeroed in `finally` blocks throughout
  (`Wipe.java:13-26`, `PasswordHasher.java:73-78, 103-107, 166-168`,
  `SessionService.java:105-109`, `AccountService.java:138-140, 214-216`,
  `App.java:102-104, 142-145, 182-187`); UTF-8 encoding goes through a `CharBuffer` so no
  `String` copy of the password is created on the common path
  (`PasswordHasher.java:172-189`). The two residual exposures (the rare non-NFC
  normalisation path at `InputValidator.java:207-211` and the cookie `String` at
  `SessionCookie.java:44`) are unavoidable with the platform APIs used and are documented in
  the code.
- **Error handling / information disclosure (CWE-209/CWE-248):** stack traces go only to the
  owner-only log; the console gets generic sentences, and `ValidationException` messages are
  format-only (`App.java:98-101, 134-141, 178-181`, `ValidationException.java:3-7`).
- **Insecure deserialization (CWE-502):** no Java serialization, XML, YAML or object-graph
  parsing exists anywhere in the codebase; the only parsed external formats are the PHC hash
  string and the environment variables, both handled with strict bounded parsers.
- **Dependency and build provenance (CWE-1104/CWE-494):** versions are pinned (Bouncy Castle
  1.79, sqlite-jdbc 3.47.1.0, slf4j-nop 2.0.16), the only repository is Maven Central over
  HTTPS with `checksumPolicy=fail` and snapshots disabled, and no known-vulnerable advisory
  was identified for the pinned versions (`pom.xml:16-31`).
